* Republish the dashboard when the mount moves, not only on a human push

The published site is stuck on claudinite-dashboard v10 while main's mount
carries v12, so the fleet grid still shows the "mount has not converged in
N days" verdict v11 removed. Nothing is wrong with the page: the deploy
never fires. Claudinite's update PRs are auto-merged by github-actions[bot],
and a push made with GITHUB_TOKEN triggers no workflow, so every converge
lands without a build.

The catch-up follows the vendored scheduler, which is this repo's one
permitted cron, and asks on each of its wake-ups whether the page's sources
have moved since the last successful deploy — so the hourly cadence costs a
cache lookup rather than an hourly republish of identical bytes.

* Republish the dashboard when the mount moves, not only on a human push

The published site is stuck on claudinite-dashboard v10 while main's mount
carries v12, so the fleet grid still shows the "mount has not converged in
N days" verdict v11 removed. Nothing is wrong with the page: the deploy
never fires. Claudinite's update PRs are auto-merged by github-actions[bot],
and a push made with GITHUB_TOKEN triggers no workflow, so every converge
lands without a build.

The catch-up follows the vendored scheduler, which is this repo's one
permitted cron, and asks on each of its wake-ups whether the page's sources
have moved since the last successful deploy — so the hourly cadence costs a
cache lookup rather than an hourly republish of identical bytes.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01TVvAw1PXq9SsUeM5W4qs5V

* Hash every generated artifact, not the roster by name

The already-deployed gate hashed `usage-fleet.GENERATED.json` because that
is what this deployment's roster happens to be called — but the roster's
file name is per-deployment config, and a member list that changed under a
different name would leave the site serving the old one. The glob is
over-inclusive by design: an extra rebuild costs one run, a missed one
costs a stale page.

Keeps this file identical to the pack's stub below its header.

The live canary caught this on the merge commit, and nothing in the suite could
have: a real member converged and its mount failed its own self-test.

The engine and pack lanes deliver on separate cycles. The `engine/scheduler/`
shims are engine-lane files that re-export a pack, so a member that converged
its engine first held a shim pointing at a pack its mount did not carry yet.
The old dashboard version it still had imports `engine/scheduler/queue/work-item.mjs`
by name; the shim there resolved to nothing; the pack failed to load; the
self-test gate refused to land the converge — which also meant the member could
not receive the pack that would have fixed it.

A shim and its target are one unit, so the lane that ships one ships the other:
`isEngineFile` carries `packs/claudinite-tasks/` for as long as the shims exist,
removed with them.

The test that was missing asserts the invariant rather than this instance: every
import in the engine lane must resolve INSIDE the engine lane. The fielded-import
scan could not see it — it asks whether a path resolves in the canon, which it
did — and the rehearsal fixtures are built from the current canon, so none of
them holds the older pack that made the window visible.

Verified against the real canary rather than a fixture: both flows converge ok,
the member's own sweep is clean, and the exact `run:` line its workflow carries
(`.claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/queue/scheduler-run.mjs`) still executes as
the program through the shim.

Refs #1317

`.claudinite-checks.json` becomes `.claudinite-settings.json`: it has not been
a file of checks since it started carrying the pack declaration, the scheduler
anchor, the installed versions and the delivery preference.

Four shape changes ride with the rename:

- A pack's installed version moves onto that pack's own entry (`version`). The
  central `claudinite.packVersions` map it replaces was keyed by an id nothing
  else in the file had to agree with, so a rename left a version pricing a pack
  the declaration no longer named (#1041).
- The `maintenance` block goes. `mechanism` recorded a rollout that finished —
  its only rival was deleted in #768 Phase 5 — and `delivery` was materialized
  into every declaration to say what every member already wanted. It becomes an
  override: `dailyClaudiniteUpdatesRequirePrReview: true` leaves the update PR
  for a human, and absence lands it.
- `taskScheduler.endpoints` becomes `agenticTaskInvocationEndpoints`, which
  says which endpoints these are.
- The `claudinite` block dissolves: `engineVersion` bubbles to the top level,
  and `updated`/`ref` are deleted. Both held the provenance of the last FULL
  re-vendor rather than of the current mount, so a member converging nightly
  read as months stale (#1065, #786). Their four readers move to the versions:
  the anti-rewind guard compares versions directly and needs no git history,
  the update precondition takes newness from the mount's own movement in the
  signal window, the sheepdog freshness sweep drops `ref-not-on-trunk` and its
  per-member canon compare, and the dashboard's converged tile is dropped and
  named as absent rather than approximated (#1001, #1008).

The rename is the migration boundary, which is what lets this land in one pass:
every reader tries both names, so a member is read correctly whether or not the
record has reached it, and `engine/migrations/2026-08-23-settings-file-rename`
renames and reshapes each member's file on its own converge. Phase 3 deletes
the tolerance, gated on no member still carrying the old name.

* Collapse the frequency vocabulary, with one normalization door at the load point

`hourly` cannot mean anything under a cron that fires twice a day, and the
`daily±Nh` offsets staggered dependent tasks by clock hour where `after:`
declares the same intent and actually enforces it. FREQUENCIES becomes
daily/weekly/monthly/manual.

THE DOOR IS AT DECLARATION LOAD, in normalizeTaskDeclaration — not in the
calendar. A frequency is read by more than the anchor: periodMs feeds the
janitor's stale-ready bound and the precondition's signal window, so
normalizing only anchorInstant would judge a task that now runs daily stale
after two HOURS, parking it needs-human on exactly the members the tolerance
exists for. The tolerance is permanent, not a window: a task declaration is
member-owned data no vendoring pass rewrites. The author-time
declaration-shape check is what stops a NEW declaration naming a retired
token.

Four declarations move. `update` daily-2h -> daily (the chain head).
`growth-extract` daily-1h -> daily, already carrying the `after:` that ordered
it. `fleet-digest` daily+1h -> daily plus `after:` naming the three sheepdog
sweeps — inert where that pack is not declared, and unlike the offset it holds
when a sweep runs long. `usage-fold` hourly -> daily, and its WINDOW_DAYS with
it: sized to an hour while the task anchors daily, the "session captured" arm
never fires again and a repo whose only movement is commit-less sessions
silently stops folding.

The cross-repo half `after:` cannot express — members extract, then this repo's
growth-promote reads what merged on their mains — moves to this repo's own
dailyHour, now 5 against members' default 4. growth-promote also declares
`after:` for the within-repo half.

The simulator models the door too, and the scenarios that asserted the old
vocabulary move with it: S1', S22, S28, S34, S65, S67 re-derived, and S70
becomes the door's own scenario. S34 now settles a whole morning in one drain
and S65's day costs 28 invocations instead of 29 — the collapse paying for
itself in scenarios that predate it. S67's slip against the hourly grid is now
zero: the 22 extra runs bought latency for ad-hoc work and nothing for the
schedule. `monthly` is modeled rather than throwing.

Refs #1225

* Take the cron to two ticks a day, both derived from the repo's dailyHour

hashedCron returns ` ,<(dailyHour+12)%24> * * *`. The anchor
tick covers every occurrence the calendar can produce — daily, weekly and
monthly all resolve to dailyHour — and the drain tick twelve hours later
carries the work that has no anchor: adopting a marked issue, releasing a
Not-before, reclaiming a dead claim.

Both hours come from the repo's own taskScheduler.dailyHour, threaded through
convergeWiring, the pack-update lane and bootstrap. Pinning them to a constant
would fire every task before its anchor on any member that moved its schedule,
landing all of them a day late forever with nothing going red — so the
rehearsal gains a `custom-anchor-hour` shape (dailyHour 9, still on the hourly
cron) and converge-wiring asserts the hours that actually land.

`dailyHour` defaults rather than being required: a member's vendored worker is
a cycle stale and may still call hashedCron with one argument, and it must get
the default-schedule answer rather than an undefined that writes a cron GitHub
rejects. That default is duplicated from calendar.mjs because hash-minute.mjs
imports nothing by contract, so a drift guard reads the two together.

scheduler-workflow-shape accepts both forms. `.github/workflows/` is the one
path a converge cannot push, so a member holds its hourly cron until its
apply-stage PR lands; going red in that window would fire the check on every
member the change has not reached yet.

The canon's own workflow copy moves in this commit too — it is hand-maintained,
has no converge, and drifts invisibly otherwise. It anchors at 5 against
members' default 4, so growth-promote reads local packs their extracts have
already merged.

Refs #1231

* Rename the ordering field: after -> schedule_after

The bare preposition invited reading the field as a time. It is not one — its
value is a list of `/` ids, and what it steers is when the item is
scheduled onto an executor: `pickOrder` is a scheduler in the dispatch sense,
deciding what runs next among runnable items, and this field is how a task says
"not while those are live".

The door already existed for exactly this. `LEGACY_FIELDS` in
normalizeTaskDeclaration is the same mechanism that carries agent_preprocessing
-> code_work, so `after` normalizes at load and a member's own task file keeps
its ordering rather than silently losing it. The rename is permanent tolerance,
not a migration window: a task declaration is member-owned data no vendoring
pass rewrites. task-declaration-shape draws an ADVISORY rename beside the
code-work one, for the same reason — the runtime still honours the old spelling,
so a member's vendor refresh must not turn its CI red over a file nobody has
edited.

Its regex is anchored on a non-word character before the key, so it cannot match
the canonical spelling's own tail — the failure the first draft of this commit
actually made, when a repo-wide sweep rewrote the finding's own remedy into
"rename schedule_after to schedule_after".

Three declarations, both engine readers, the simulator's two readers and the
prose across DESIGN/SCENARIOS/writing-tasks move with it. The sim's readers were
the silent half: the sweep renamed the cast's declarations and left
`registry.get(...)?.after`, which three scenarios caught.

Co-authored-by: Claude "},"path":".github/workflows/canary-rehearsal.yml","html_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/actions/runs/32566810812","actor":{"login":"missingbulb","id":73882448,"profile_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/73882448?v=4"},"triggering_actor":{"login":"missingbulb","id":73882448,"profile_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/73882448?v=4"},"created_at":"2026-08-22T10:08:06Z","updated_at":"2026-08-22T10:08:21Z","run_started_at":"2026-08-22T10:08:06Z"},{"id":32371130795,"name":"Canary rehearsal","display_title":"Canary rehearsal","workflow_id":324780266,"run_number":174,"run_attempt":1,"event":"workflow_dispatch","status":"completed","conclusion":"success","head_branch":"claude/version-format-migration-1mb5vp","head_sha":"1f05d43c615eefa653e638c04fb457f6f845a403","head_commit":{"message":"Engine and pack versions become date-anchored `.`

Versions were a plain monotonic counter, which orders releases but says
nothing about when one was cut: a member stamped at 6 against a canon at 13
is behind by an unknown amount of time, and every fleet surface reporting
that gap makes a reader go and date it by hand.

`engine/version.mjs` now owns the format beside the constant it describes —
`60820.1`, where the day part is `(year - 2020) * 10000 + month * 100 + day`
and the second part is the running number of versions cut on that day. The
year is anchored on 2020 rather than taken as its last digit so the ordering
survives 2030, and a version is a STRING because `60820.10` and `60820.1`
are different versions and the same float.

Every reader accepts a legacy integer as well, parsed as `.0` — below

Nothing had converged a member's `.github/workflows/claudinite-scheduler.yml`
since the fleet flipped to `updates`. `isPackFile` covers `packs//` and
nothing outside the mount; the engine flow passes `{ workflows: false }` because
its token is refused there; baselining, which used to do it, was retired in
Phase 5 and nothing replaced it. So every member's wiring froze at whatever
baselining last wrote — including the hashed cron minute and the union of every
task's `required_secrets`, neither of which any future change could reach.

Worse, the pack flow announced `CLAUDINITE_CAN_WITHHOLD_WORKFLOWS: '1'` and
withheld nothing. The first record materializing a workflow would have written
it, the worker's `git add -A` would have staged it, and GitHub's refusal would
have rejected the whole ref — failing the entire update, not just that file.

diverted to `.claudinite/pending-workflows/`, a path the Action token can push,

because this is the one point in the cycle that sees the task set it just
vendored. Staged files are swept when no longer owed, so the directory is empty
exactly when nothing is outstanding — which makes "did the stage actually run"
a question with an answer.

The content travels through the REPOSITORY, not the dispatch. That is the
scheduler's rule for the code→agent boundary: a request payload carries
identifiers and the name of the condition, never findings and never
instructions. Obeying it buys two things worth more than the shortcut — the
withheld workflow lands in the update's own PR diff where a human reviews it
before any session runs, and it survives a session that never ran.

Which retired `applyStageBrief`. It rendered instructions into the payload,
nothing read them, and they restated task.md §2-5 from a second home no test
could catch drifting. The apply stage is now told why by `reason.detail`, what
to do by task.md, and what to do it to by the branch — the staged files and the
migration record the reason names.

input.body:
Every member's executor workflow is now one workflow-file change away from being parked by GitHub with:

> GitHub detected that this workflow file may be malicious. It will not run until someone with write access approves it.

A parked run creates **zero jobs** and concludes `action_required` in about a second, so from the queue's side the item simply never gets picked up — no error, no failure, nothing red. It reads exactly like a settings problem, which is how I first mis-diagnosed it in #1330.

## What triggers it

`packs/claudinite-tasks/stubs/claudinite-executor.yml:52`, and the canon's own copy at the same line:

```yaml
CLAUDINITE_SECRETS: ${{ toJSON(secrets) }}
```

Serialising the entire secrets context into an environment variable is the canonical exfiltration shape, and GitHub's malicious-workflow detection flags it. (The banner does not name the line; that it is this one is inferred from the timing below plus the pattern being the only thing in the file that fits.)

## The timing, which is unambiguous

| When (UTC) | What |
|---|---|
| 2026-08-24 06:07:55 | Claudinite's executor — last `success` |
| 2026-08-24 08:31:14 | `fd4cb68` merges #1302, adding the `toJSON(secrets)` line |
| 2026-08-24 08:33:31 | Claudinite's executor — first `action_required`, two minutes later |
| 2026-08-24 11:24, 11:27 | Shepherd's executor — `success`, twice |
| 2026-08-24 11:48 onward | Shepherd's executor — `action_required` on every run, bot- and owner-triggered alike |

**This predates the #1317 extraction and is unrelated to it.** The extraction carried the line forward unchanged, which was right — but see the L2 consequence below.

## Why it matters more than one approval

- The line is in the **stub every member is scaffolded with**, so this is not two repos, it is the fleet.
- The whole point of the queue is unattended work. A gate that needs a person to press *Approve and run* is the one thing the mechanism cannot absorb.
- It is **silent**. `action_required` with zero jobs is indistinguishable from "nothing was pickable" unless you go looking at run conclusions, and the fleet's own health signals read stamps, not run states.
- **#1317's L2 (#1331) will trip it on all 14 members.** L2 hand-edits both workflow files in every member; each edit re-exposes the file to the scan. That turns a per-repo mechanical edit into a per-repo edit *plus* a manual approval, and any member missed sits with a stalled queue and nothing red to show for it.

## What #1302 was solving, and a shape that keeps it

#1302's problem was real: naming secrets one by one meant every new secret needed a human-merged PR in every member, and `.github/workflows/` is the one path a converge cannot push. Reverting reinstates exactly that.

Three ways out, in the order I'd weigh them:

1. **One dedicated secret holding a JSON blob.** The workflow line becomes `CLAUDINITE_SECRETS: ${{ secrets.CLAUDINITE_SECRETS }}` — static, no `toJSON`, and still one line that never changes when a task needs a new value, because the value lives inside that one secret rather than in the YAML. Keeps #1302's property and drops the flagged pattern.
2. **Name the secrets explicitly again.** Safe, and gives back the fleet-wide-PR-per-secret cost #1302 removed.
3. **Keep it and absorb the approvals.** Cheapest today, and it makes an unattended fleet depend on someone noticing a silent park.

Option 1 needs checking against what `secrets-bag.mjs` actually reads before it is more than a sketch.

Blocked-by: nothing — but #1331 should not start until this is decided, or L2 will multiply it by fourteen.

    one path a converge cannot write, so every new secret needed a human-merged PR

    carries `CLAUDINITE_SECRETS: ${{ toJSON(secrets) }}` and stops tracking
    declarations. secrets-bag.mjs is the only reader.
    
    The selection moves inward, which tightens rather than loosens it: code-work
    used to inherit the executor's whole environment and see every stamped secret,
    though only 6 of 22 code-work tasks declare one. It now gets exactly the names
    its own declaration lists, which is what DESIGN §14.4 always claimed.
    
    A member's live executor moves only by human-merged PR, so the reader falls back
    to the plain environment when no bag is present; a rehearsal fixture holds that
    shape. Retiring the fallback is gated on no member still stamping, not a date.

Name the executor's secrets again; `toJSON(secrets)` is what GitHub flags

Reverses #1301's one-line secret bag, on the owner's call.

The line `CLAUDINITE_SECRETS: ${{ toJSON(secrets) }}` is the shape GitHub's
malicious-workflow detection flags. A flagged workflow does not run until a
person clicks Approve, and it parks with zero jobs — so from the queue's side it
is indistinguishable from "nothing was pickable". An unattended fleet can
neither absorb that nor notice it. It began two minutes after #1302 merged and
had been silently eating executor runs in the canon and in Shepherd since.

So the executor workflow lists each secret again, and the wiring converge — now
the tasks pack's converge-workflows.mjs — regenerates that list at the
`# claudinite:secrets` marker from every declared task's `required_secrets` plus
the configured endpoint tokens.

The cost this reinstates is the one #1301 removed and is not pretended away: the
file becomes a function of the task set, `.github/workflows/` is the one path a
converge cannot write, and a NEW secret therefore needs a human-merged PR in
every member — the coupling that wedged one in #1296. The trade is deliberate: a
rare human-merged PR beats a permanent human click on every run.

secrets-bag.mjs stays. Its selection — a task's code-work sees exactly the names
its own declaration lists, rather than inheriting the executor's whole
environment — was #1301's other half, it is independent of how the secrets
arrive, and it keeps working off the plain environment. Its bag reader stays too,
because every member carries the bag-setting workflow until its own PR lands.

Both windows now have a rehearsal fixture: `stamping-executor` for the named
shape, and a new `bag-executor` for the members sitting in the reversal's own
window. A stub guard pins `toJSON(secrets)` out of both stubs, seen to fail with
the line put back.

The design docs that stated #1301's decision now state this one, with what it
costs.

Refs #1336

file.content:
# A thin wrapper: every decision lives in the engine modules named in the `run:`
# lines below, which converge nightly — this file does not, so it must not grow
# logic. It carries no cron; the scheduler workflow's drain is the guaranteed
# delivery and a label event is latency sugar.
name: Claudinite executor

on:
  issues:
    types: [labeled]
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      continuation_depth:
        description: 'How many dead runs this chain has continued through — set by the continuation job below, never by hand'
        required: false
        type: string

permissions:
  contents: write
  issues: write
  pull-requests: write
  actions: write

jobs:
  execute:
    # A workflow's event trigger names label strings LITERALLY — nothing here
    # decodes — so both ready spellings must appear for as long as any fielded
    # engine writes the legacy one (#1119).
    if: >-
      github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch'
      || github.event.label.name == 'task:status:waiting-for-executor'
      || github.event.label.name == 'task:ready'
      || github.event.label.name == 'task:urgent'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    # A backstop against a wedged runner, well clear of any declared
    # `code_work_timeout`; the heartbeat's leash is what bounds real work.
    timeout-minutes: 350
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version: 24
      - name: Pick up and execute ready work
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          CLAUDINITE_TASKS_SUSPEND_ALL: ${{ vars.CLAUDINITE_TASKS_SUSPEND_ALL }}
          # EVERY SECRET, IN ONE STATIC LINE (#1301). Actions has no way to export
          # the secrets context as variables, and naming them one by one made this
          # file a function of the task set — which wedges members, because a
          # converge cannot write .github/workflows/ and only a human-merged PR
          # moves it (#1296). secrets-bag.mjs is the only reader; the executor hands
          # each task just the names its own declaration lists.
          CLAUDINITE_SECRETS: ${{ toJSON(secrets) }}
        run: node .claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/queue/executor.mjs

  continue-the-chain:
    needs: execute
    if: failure() || cancelled()
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      actions: write
      issues: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version: 24
      - name: Continue the drain, or escalate a chain that keeps dying
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          CLAUDINITE_CONTINUATION_DEPTH: ${{ inputs.continuation_depth }}
        run: node .claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/queue/executor-continuation.mjs

---
name: merge-to-main
description: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner says "LGTM" or asks to merge/land the current branch or PR into main.
---

# Merge to main

If the project's own `CLAUDE.md` names a merge-policy file, that file overrides the divergent
points below (merge method, CI gating). Don't go hunting for one it doesn't name.

1. Load `create_pull_request` + `merge_pull_request` in one `ToolSearch`.
2. No PR open for the branch? `create_pull_request` (base `main`), body ending `Closes #<issue>`.
3. If the PR has check runs, wait for them to pass. None — merge without waiting.
4. `merge_pull_request`, `merge_method: squash`, title `<subject> (#<pr>)`. Don't pre-read
   mergeability; the call fails loudly.
5. Sync local `main`: `git checkout main && git pull origin main`.
6. Capture the conversation:
   `node .claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`
   (in the canon repo: `node packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`). Skip only if
   the repo doesn't declare `claudinite-growth`. A later merge in the same session runs it again.
7. Run the basics pack's
   [verify-in-production](../../../basics/skills/verify-in-production/SKILL.md) skill, unasked.
   This step is that skill's **only** trigger — it files against what the squash actually landed,
   which is why it runs here and not when the code was written or the PR opened. It decides
   whether this change needs a production check at all — most don't — and files the issue that
   comes back once the change is live. Never offer the owner to check later instead.

Don't re-read the issue to confirm it closed — `Closes #<issue>` does that on merge.

skills.name: verify-in-production
skills.content:
Base directory for this skill: /home/user/Claudinite/.claude/skills/verify-in-production

# Verify in production

A change is finished when someone has watched it work. Most changes you can watch **now**, and
that is the rule — this skill is only for the rest: a change whose proof lives somewhere the
repo cannot see yet. You are filing the proof, not doing the work — and the proof itself runs
unattended: an automatic check, end to end, with a person entering
only where no automatic check can exist.

## When it fires: after the merge, never before

**The PR must have merged.** This skill runs as a step of the merge, unasked — `merge-to-main`
calls it once the squash has landed — and at no other moment. Not when the code is written, not
when the PR opens, not while review is in flight.

The reason is that a PR can be **rejected**, and a branch that is still open can be rewritten
under you. Both leave a verification whose premise never reached `main`:

- A **rewritten branch** makes the brief describe a change that no longer exists. #1121 was filed
  against a scope its PR then dropped; the verification was moot before the merge it waited on.
- A **rejected PR** is worse, because the queue cannot tell it from a merge. A blocked item
  releases on its blocker being *closed*, and nothing reads `merged` — so the item goes ready,
  reads an `In-production-when:` that can never become true, pushes `Not-before:` forward by
  `Retry-every:` without comment, and repeats indefinitely. No janitor rule reclaims it: the
  stale-ready sweep cannot see an item sleeping on a future `Not-before`, and the
  stuck-dependency sweep exempts an item whose blockers have closed.

So there is no such thing as filing this early and letting the queue sort it out. Wait for the
merge, then read **what actually landed** — the merged diff, not the branch you remember writing.

## First: does this file anything at all?

Most changes **file nothing.** Run the test in this order and stop at the first answer:

1. **Did you watch it work in this session?** Then it is proven. File nothing.
2. **Did a test that ran prove it?** A unit test, a CI job, an executable-requirements or UI
   test covering exactly the behaviour that changed. File nothing — the suite is the mechanism
   that comes back.
3. **Does the change have an observable effect at all?** A comment, a design doc, a README, a
   rename with no behavioural edge, a refactor a passing suite already pins. File nothing.
4. **Otherwise: where does its effect first become observable?** If the answer is a place and a
   moment — a member repo once it converges, a site once it deploys, a session once it reloads
   its rules — that is what you file.

The bar is *could not be watched now*, not *would be nice to double-check*. A verification
filed for a change already covered by a test is a wasted run re-proving what the suite proved.

## What you file

**A deferred request** — the same ad-hoc lane `/do-later` rides, so the queue does the waiting,
the running and the lifecycle; nothing here adds machinery beside it. One issue, titled
`Verify in production: <the change, in a few words>`, its body the whole brief: the run that
verifies will never see this conversation and may be days away. Say what changed and why it
could not be watched now, then, each spelled verbatim on its own line:

```
Original-issue: #<the change's issue>
In-production-when: <the concrete artifact to read, and what makes it true>
Verify: <what to observe, and what counts as a pass>
Not-before: <ISO instant just past the expected release>
Retry-every: <how far to push Not-before when not yet live, e.g. 1 day>
```

No `Blocked-by:`. You are filing after the merge, so the change's PR has already closed and
there is nothing left to wait on but the release itself.

- **`Original-issue:`** is where a failure lands — the issue the change was done under, which
  the run reopens if the verification fails. Make the verification that issue's **sub-issue**
  too (`mcp__github__sub_issue_write`, method `add`, `issue_number` the original,
  `sub_issue_id` the **id** the create call returned, not its number), so the change it proves
  shows what is still unproven about it — [RULES.md](../../RULES.md)' *Filing an issue that
  belongs under another*, applied where there is no PR left to carry the link.
- **`In-production-when:`** names a thing to *read*, never a duration to wait. "`missingbulb/Shepherd`'s
  `.claudinite-settings.json` stamps `packVersions.tidy-repo` at 8 or higher." "The live site's
  `/version.json` reports a version past 4.2.0." "Any session started after this landed — check
  the vendored copy under `.claudinite/shared/` carries the new text." A merge is not a
  production condition, and neither is elapsed time.
- **`Verify:`** is an assertion with a pass condition, not a topic — and a read an **unattended
  run can make**: an API response, a file at a URL, an issue's state. "Issue #100 on that repo
  is closed with a comment citing the scheduler runs" beats "check tidy-issues works". Only where no
  automatic check can exist may `Verify:` name a person's step, spelled out exactly.
- **`Not-before:`** is the queue's own wait field: adoption holds the run until the moment has
  passed. Aim it just past the release you expect — the re-arm covers a miss, so don't pad it.
- **`Retry-every:`** is the extension you are prescribing: when the run finds the change not
  yet live, it pushes `Not-before:` forward by exactly this much. Size it to the release you
  wait on — a nightly converge retries daily, a next-session rule in minutes.

Then the mark, as `/do-later` applies it: **`task:origin:ad-hoc`**, the one label the scheduler
run adopts. Beside it, in the body, **`Model: sonnet`** (reading a live artifact and judging an
assertion against it). Never `Automerge:` — a verification has nothing to merge. If the mark
doesn't exist in the repo yet, say so and leave the issue — it appears on the next scheduler run.

## Tell the run how to converge

End the body with instructions to the run itself — the issue is its whole brief, and the run
decides nothing: it executes this playbook.

1. Read `In-production-when:` against the real artifact. Never infer it from a merge, a green
   run, or elapsed time.
2. **Live** → run `Verify:`. Passes: comment the evidence actually read (the version, the value,
   the URL) and close this issue as completed. Fails: reopen `Original-issue:` with a comment
   saying what was asserted, what happened instead and where you read it; comment here linking
   that; close this issue as completed — the verification did its job by finding the fault.
3. **Not yet live** → push `Not-before:` forward by `Retry-every:`, **clear the issue's
   `task:status:*` label** (clearing the status is the whole of the re-ask — the mark stays on
   for life), and leave the issue open. The next scheduler run re-adopts it, and the bumped
   field holds it until the new moment. No comment; the bumped field is the record.

## Then say what you filed

One line back to the owner: the issue link, what it waits on, and its retry cadence.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files and comment-only changes.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

input.body:
Reverses #1301's one-line secret bag, on the owner's call.

## What was wrong

`CLAUDINITE_SECRETS: ${{ toJSON(secrets) }}` is the shape GitHub's malicious-workflow detection flags. A flagged workflow does not run until a person clicks **Approve**, and it parks with **zero jobs** — from the queue's side that is indistinguishable from "nothing was pickable". An unattended fleet can neither absorb that nor notice it. It started two minutes after #1302 merged (fd4cb68 at 08:31:14 UTC; first park 08:33:31 UTC) and had been silently eating executor runs in the canon and in Shepherd ever since — it is why L1's fleet-baseline saw 8 of 13 members fail to reach canon.

## What this does

- The executor workflow lists each secret by name again, and the wiring converge — now the tasks pack's `converge-workflows.mjs` — regenerates that list at the `# claudinite:secrets` marker from every declared task's `required_secrets` plus the configured endpoint tokens.
- **The cost this reinstates is not pretended away**: the file becomes a function of the task set, `.github/workflows/` is the one path a converge cannot write, and a NEW secret therefore needs a human-merged PR in every member — the coupling that wedged one in #1296. The owner took that trade explicitly: a rare human-merged PR beats a permanent human click on every run.
- `queue/secrets-bag.mjs` **stays**. Its selection — a task's code-work sees exactly the names its own declaration lists, rather than inheriting the executor's whole environment — was #1301's other half, is independent of how the secrets arrive, and keeps working off the plain environment. Its bag *reader* stays too, because every member carries the bag-setting workflow until its own PR lands; retiring it is gated on no member still stamping a bag, a converge-confirmable condition, never a date.
- Both windows now have a rehearsal fixture: `stamping-executor` for the named shape, and a new `bag-executor` for members sitting inside this reversal's own window.
- A stub guard pins `toJSON(secrets)` out of both stubs — seen to fail with the line put back.
- The design docs that stated #1301's decision now state this one, with what it costs.

## Folders touched

```
.github/workflows/     executor workflow names its secrets again, at the marker
docs/                  tasks-dispatch and task-code-work DESIGNs restate the decision
engine/                converge-wiring hands the workflow half its config
packs/claudinite-tasks/  converge-workflows regenerates the secret list; secrets-bag
                         keeps selection + a transitional bag reader; stub + tests
vendoring/             rehearsal fixtures gain bag-executor
```

## Verification

`node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')` → exit 0, 0 failures. `check_the_work` → 0 blocking. `check_the_world` → 0 blocking.

Closes #1336

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.

- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files and comment-only changes.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.
